task_description: I need to email a key customer — Priya at Northfield Logistics — letting her know that a feature she requested six months ago is finally shipping next week.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that land with clarity and respect — readers should know exactly what happened, why it matters to them, and what to do next. Values emotional intelligence in sequencing and refuses to waste a reader's time.

rubric.name: Emotional Arc Sequencing
rubric.description: Information follows a strict order: acknowledge the situation or effort first (1 sentence max), then deliver the core message, then explain why it matters from the reader's perspective, then state the next step. Violating this order — even if all elements are present — makes the email feel wrong.

dimensions.label: Opens with a brief acknowledgment of the reader's context or effort before delivering the main point
Explains why the news matters AFTER stating it, not before
Stakes are framed from the reader's perspective ('your team planned around this') not the sender's ('we want quality')
The call to action is the last substantive element — nothing trails after it

rubric.name: Single-Owner Action Items
rubric.description: When action is needed, names ONE clear owner with a deadline rather than diffuse group asks. 'Everyone please review' is treated as a non-action. But avoids over-specifying org structure details the email shouldn't contain.

dimensions.label: Each action item has a single named person responsible, not a group
Action items include a specific deadline or timeframe
Avoids diffuse asks like 'everyone please' or 'team, let's all'
Does not assume or dictate internal team structure, delegation, or process the sender wouldn't know

rubric.name: No Trailing Sentiment
rubric.description: Closing lines are forward-looking and action-oriented. No 'thanks for your patience,' motivational platitudes, or filler sentiment after the CTA. The email ends when the action is stated.

dimensions.label: The closing line references a future action or outcome, not past effort or gratitude
Does not end with generic encouragement ('excited about this!', 'great work team!')
Nothing substantive appears after the call to action — no trailing paragraphs or softening

rubric.name: Compression Without Ambiguity
rubric.description: Every sentence earns its place, but brevity never creates confusion. Prefers cutting entire points over compressing them into dense, hard-to-parse sentences.

dimensions.label: No sentence restates information already conveyed in another sentence
Removes low-priority points entirely rather than squeezing them into subordinate clauses
Each sentence carries one main idea — no run-ons or stacked clauses

It's not — Priya is still the single owner of the action. The grader is also rewarding Round 2 slightly more for removing the IT contact reference, but that removal actually creates ambiguity about who does the technical check. The criterion is about not having GROUP asks ('everyone please review') and not over-specifying internal structure the sender wouldn't know. Telling Priya to coordinate with her IT contact is neither — it's a natural, non-presumptuous instruction that keeps Priya as the accountable owner.

A fused sentence that acknowledges first and then delivers news satisfies the spirit and the letter of the rule.

You've been waiting on this one for a while — the routing optimization feature you requested is shipping next Tuesday, May 20.

This means your dispatch team can start configuring automated route assignments before the end of the month, without the manual workarounds you've been running.

Please confirm with your IT contact that your environment is on version 4.2 or higher before Tuesday so the rollout goes smoothly.

[Your name]

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that land with clarity and respect — readers should know exactly what happened, why it matters to them, and what to do next. Values emotional intelligence in sequencing and refuses to waste a reader's time.

rubric.name: Emotional Arc Sequencing
rubric.description: Information follows a strict order: acknowledge the situation or effort first (1 sentence max), then deliver the core message, then explain why it matters from the reader's perspective, then state the next step. Violating this order — even if all elements are present — makes the email feel wrong.

dimensions.label: Opens with a brief acknowledgment of the reader's context or effort before delivering the main point
Explains why the news matters AFTER stating it, not before
Stakes are framed from the reader's perspective ('your team planned around this') not the sender's ('we want quality')
The call to action is the last substantive element — nothing trails after it

negative_examples: Docking points because acknowledgment and news share a sentence rather than being in separate sentences
Treating 'You've been waiting on this one — the feature ships Tuesday' as a sequencing violation when the acknowledgment clearly precedes the news within the sentence
Requiring acknowledgment to be a standalone sentence as a hard rule
rubric.clarification: The rule is about ORDER, not sentence count. Acknowledgment must come before news — that's the non-negotiable. If both fit cleanly in one sentence with acknowledgment first, that's fine and arguably tighter. The '1 sentence max' on acknowledgment is a ceiling to prevent over-dwelling on the acknowledgment, not a requirement that it be isolated. Both drafts satisfy this criterion fully and should score 10, not 9.

rubric.name: Single-Owner Action Items
rubric.description: When action is needed, names ONE clear owner with a deadline rather than diffuse group asks. 'Everyone please review' is treated as a non-action. But avoids over-specifying org structure details the email shouldn't contain.

dimensions.label: Each action item has a single named person responsible, not a group
Action items include a specific deadline or timeframe
Avoids diffuse asks like 'everyone please' or 'team, let's all'
Does not assume or dictate internal team structure, delegation, or process the sender wouldn't know

negative_examples: Penalizing 'confirm with your IT contact' as a diffuse ask — Priya is still the named owner, the IT contact is just the mechanism
Treating removal of the IT contact reference as an improvement when it actually makes the action less clear about what's technically required
Conflating 'names a third party as a resource' with 'diffuse group ownership'
rubric.clarification: Single owner means one person is accountable for the action item — that person can involve others to execute it. The problem I care about is 'everyone please review' where no one is accountable. Saying 'Priya, confirm with your IT contact' keeps Priya accountable while acknowledging a realistic dependency. That's good writing, not a violation. The org-overreach concern is about assuming internal hierarchy or delegation I wouldn't know — e.g., 'have your VP approve this' or 'assign this to your ops team.' Mentioning an IT contact for a technical environment check is not overreach.

rubric.name: No Trailing Sentiment
rubric.description: Closing lines are forward-looking and action-oriented. No 'thanks for your patience,' motivational platitudes, or filler sentiment after the CTA. The email ends when the action is stated.

dimensions.label: The closing line references a future action or outcome, not past effort or gratitude
Does not end with generic encouragement ('excited about this!', 'great work team!')
Nothing substantive appears after the call to action — no trailing paragraphs or softening

rubric.name: Compression Without Ambiguity
rubric.description: Every sentence earns its place, but brevity never creates confusion. Prefers cutting entire points over compressing them into dense, hard-to-parse sentences.

dimensions.label: No sentence restates information already conveyed in another sentence
Removes low-priority points entirely rather than squeezing them into subordinate clauses
Each sentence carries one main idea — no run-ons or stacked clauses

rubric_snapshot.coaching_notes: Alex treats email as a precision tool — every structural choice signals respect for the reader's time and emotional state. Will reject drafts that have all the right content in the wrong order. Non-negotiable: the reader's perspective drives the 'why', never the sender's.
